Yesterday, I asked a [question](https://voat.co/v/AskVoat/comments/972128) and got help from lots of awesome voaters. This question helped me with a problem I noticed before. Maybe some of you attended Spanish classes before, and there is a common mistake among the students, which is confusing the j and the r sounds (most have trouble pronouncing the j). These are very different, yet somehow people don't *hear* the difference. It confused me a lot, but since I have heard some Spanish since I was a kid, I figured I was the weird one.

Now a few years later, my godfather, who lives in England, told me most people have no idea how to say his name, Didier. And his son, who lived in England his whole life, mispronounced my name. It didn't actually bothered me, I was used to some people saying it differently (I answer to both the French and the Spanish versions of my name), it just added another version to the list.

Yesterday, I performed an experiment. It turns out there are sounds you English speakers literally can't hear. When I hear the sound é, you can hear i, you, yeah... And that's fascinating. We can listen to the exact same words and hear completely different things. Our brains are shaped by the language it processed since birth, and it distorts our perceptions so instead of hearing the "right" word, you hear an approximation because some sounds don't exist for your brain.

That's the most interesting experiment I ever performed, and it wasn't even what I intended to do. Maybe I'm just an idiot, but that's the kind of things I'd like to study a bit.
